Open auditability is a parameter, and not an institution foreign to the system. It unfolds from the duty of information, objective good faith and the facilitation of defense in Article 6 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. The regime for disclosure of documents or things in Articles 396 to 400 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)<3><4>2</4></3> is the most direct route to put it into operation. It is the minimum threshold of external verifiability that turns opaque modulations into matter for adversarial debate, proof and decision.

In the Vanguard case, protection against cheating came to depend on software loaded into the core of the operating system, started with the computer and kept as a condition of enjoyment. The platform's governance thus reaches the consumer's own equipment. The interest in preserving competitive integrity is legitimate, but the question is whether it is enough to authorize this expansion without reinforced control. Articles 8, 10 and 12 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> reach the risk that the architecture transfers to the equipment, and Article 6 of Law 13,709/2018, the General Data Protection Law (LGPD)<3><4>4</4></3>, requires purpose, necessity and transparency in data processing. The point is not to assert the automatic unlawfulness of the software, but to refuse its legal immunization. Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security, and open auditability prevents the platform from hiding behind technical opacity and trade secrets.

In the same vein, the regime for the production of a document or thing provided for in Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>2</2></1> offers the most direct route to operationalize open auditability.<3>p. 659</3>

Open auditability is a parameter, and not an institution foreign to the system. It unfolds from the duty of information, objective good faith and the facilitation of defense in Article 6 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. The regime for disclosure of documents or things in Articles 396 to 400 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)<3><4>2</4></3> is the most direct route to put it into operation. It is the minimum threshold of external verifiability that turns opaque modulations into matter for adversarial debate, proof and decision.

In the Vanguard case, protection against cheating came to depend on software loaded into the core of the operating system, started with the computer and kept as a condition of enjoyment. The platform's governance thus reaches the consumer's own equipment. The interest in preserving competitive integrity is legitimate, but the question is whether it is enough to authorize this expansion without reinforced control. Articles 8, 10 and 12 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> reach the risk that the architecture transfers to the equipment, and Article 6 of Law 13,709/2018, the General Data Protection Law (LGPD)<3><4>4</4></3>, requires purpose, necessity and transparency in data processing. The point is not to assert the automatic unlawfulness of the software, but to refuse its legal immunization. Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security, and open auditability prevents the platform from hiding behind technical opacity and trade secrets.

In the same vein, the regime for the production of a document or thing provided for in Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>2</2></1> offers the most direct route to operationalize open auditability.<3>p. 659</3>

Article 31 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> requires correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information in the offer and in the presentation. Article 46 of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3> releases the consumer from obligations when there was no real opportunity to learn of them beforehand or when the wording hinders understanding. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 54 of the CDC<5><6>3</6></5> require clear adhesion contracts and highlighted limiting clauses. Article 47 of the CDC<7><8>4</8></7> requires clauses to be interpreted in the way most favorable to the consumer. This rule connects to the control of abusiveness provided for in Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<9><10>5</10></9>.

For this reason, the new function of contract law places the principle of interpretation in accordance with good faith back at the center, so that art. 47 of the CDC<1><2>4</2></1>, together with the general clause of art. 51, IV, allows the pre-drafted clauses to be interpreted<3>p. 605</3>

Article 30 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> makes all sufficiently precise information binding, and the presentation in the digital storefront may constitute an offer. Article 35 of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3> allows the consumer to demand specific relief, accept an equivalent performance or rescind the contract and claim damages. Article 38 of the CDC<5><6>3</6></5> places on whoever sponsors the advertising the burden of proving that the information is true and correct. In the curated anticipation of the offer, relevant omission appears when what is essential is moved outside the focus of the decision. Advertising is misleading when the utility or equivalence built by the promotional environment finds no verifiable correspondence in enjoyment. And it is abusive when the design systematically exploits vulnerability, compressing deliberation through artificial urgency, symbolic reward and fragmentation of the relevant conditions.
Hence the importance of art. 35 of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1><3>p. 540</3>

It is precisely for this reason that art. 38 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> proves so important here. The burden of proving the truthfulness and correctness of the advertising information or communication lies with whoever sponsors it<3>p. 627</3>

Situation e) · 7.1.2 of the thesis

Open auditability is a parameter, and not an institution foreign to the system. It unfolds from the duty of information, objective good faith and the facilitation of defense in Article 6 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. The regime for disclosure of documents or things in Articles 396 to 400 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC)<3><4>2</4></3> is the most direct route to put it into operation. It is the minimum threshold of external verifiability that turns opaque modulations into matter for adversarial debate, proof and decision.

In the Vanguard case, protection against cheating came to depend on software loaded into the core of the operating system, started with the computer and kept as a condition of enjoyment. The platform's governance thus reaches the consumer's own equipment. The interest in preserving competitive integrity is legitimate, but the question is whether it is enough to authorize this expansion without reinforced control. Articles 8, 10 and 12 of the CDC<1><2>3</2></1> reach the risk that the architecture transfers to the equipment, and Article 6 of Law 13,709/2018, the General Data Protection Law (LGPD)<3><4>4</4></3>, requires purpose, necessity and transparency in data processing. The point is not to assert the automatic unlawfulness of the software, but to refuse its legal immunization. Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security, and open auditability prevents the platform from hiding behind technical opacity and trade secrets.

In the same vein, the regime for the production of a document or thing provided for in Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC<1><2>2</2></1> offers the most direct route to operationalize open auditability.<3>p. 659</3>

Article 39 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> prohibits abusive practices, including leaving performance of the obligation to the exclusive discretion of the supplier. The barrier clause, which hinders the exercise of a claim without plausible justification, runs counter to Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3>. Depending on the case, there is a defect in the service when the legal and procedural security of enjoyment is compromised. Consumer protection, as a fundamental right and a principle of the economic order, is already enough to frame private forms of government that produce broad and repeated effects on enjoyment, even though they are not to be confused with state power.

Claudia Lima Marques shows that the “barrier clause” is contrary to art. 51, IV, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, precisely because it substantially unbalances the contractual relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</4>.<5>p. 669</5>

Situation h) · 7.1.2 of the thesis

Article 39 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> prohibits abusive practices, such as taking advantage of the consumer's weakness. Article 51, item IV, of the CDC<3><4>2</4></3>, read in light of the barrier clause, makes it possible to control entire procedural arrangements designed to produce asymmetric friction. Article 84 of the CDC<5><6>3</6></5> supports specific relief, and in the face of a repeated pattern the system also calls for injunctive relief. Article 29 of the CDC<7><8>4</8></7> reaches those exposed to the platform's practices. Framing under the CDC goes through three doors. The first is the quality defect, when the program produces a relevant loss of adequacy, continuity or equivalence of enjoyment. The second is abusive practices, when artificial scarcity, fabricated urgency and asymmetric friction operate in a predictable and repeated way. The third is abusive clauses, when the program takes shape in pre-drafted terms, policies and acceptances. There is no need to leave the CDC or invent a parallel law of platforms.

Article 5, item XXIX, of the Federal Constitution<1><2>1</2></1> ties the protection of industrial creations, trademarks and other signs to the social interest and to development, and does not protect exclusivity as an end in itself. Property is subject to its social function, and consumer protection is part of the economic order. Articles 7 and 8 of Law 9,609/1998, the Software Law<3><4>2</4></3>, impose on the software supplier duties of information and of support during technical validity. Protection of computer programs in Brazil follows a special regime that is predominantly copyright-based, and not a patent logic over function, method or result, so technical control of the infrastructure does not turn into total power over the experience consumed.
